section_summary: This section contains U.S. Department of State records from August to November 1932 documenting internal political dynamics in Japan and diplomatic developments surrounding the Manchurian crisis. Primary focus is given to Foreign Minister Count Uchida's Diet speech justifying the imminent recognition of Manchukuo, along with State Department and Tokyo Embassy analyses of rampant militarism, the cultivation of war psychology, and the intimidation of civilian leaders following Premier Inukai's assassination. The records also cover the launch of Kenzo Adachi's Kokumin Domei party, circulating extremist circulars within the Japanese military, and departmental correspondence regarding official Japanese documentation.

subfiles.about: Record of Acting Secretary Castle's press conference discussing Foreign Minister Uchida's Diet address on Manchuria and the status of the Lytton Commission report.
subfiles.summary: Acting Secretary Castle's August 25, 1932 press conference on Uchida's Diet address: nothing new, aimed at the League. Recognition of Manchukuo would conflict with the Nine-Power Pact.
subfiles.title: Memorandum of the Press Conference, Thursday, August 25, 1932

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing Tokyo telegram No. 221 regarding Japanese press approval of Count Uchida's Diet address.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references Telegram No. 221 (894.032/113), August 27, 1932: Japanese press warmly welcomed Count Uchida's Diet speech.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Telegram No. 221 from Tokyo Regarding Uchida Diet Speech

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting unanimous Japanese press acclaim for Count Uchida's Diet address and the decision to recognize Manchukuo.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports the Japanese press unanimously endorsed Uchida's August 25 speech, praising its implied recognition of Manchukuo and a bold new Foreign Office policy.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 221 from Tokyo on Press Reaction to Uchida's Speech

subfiles.about: Memorandum of conversation between Under Secretary Castle and Japanese Chargé Kato, enclosing the full text of Count Uchida's Diet address.
subfiles.summary: Under Secretary William R. Castle Jr. records his conversation of August 24, 1932, with Japanese Chargé d'Affaires Sotomatsu Kato, who presented an advance copy of Foreign Minister Count Yasuye Uchida's address to the 63rd Diet. Castle expressed regret over Japan's determination to recognize Manchukuo, questioning whether the world would believe it reflected the will of the Manchurian people, and cautioned against the financial perils of prolonged military adventure. In the attached address delivered on August 25, Count Uchida justifies Japan's Manchurian campaign under the right of self-defense, denies any violation of the Anti-War Pact or Nine-Power Treaty, and asserts that recognizing Manchukuo is the sole practical means of stabilizing the Far East.
subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation with Japanese Chargé Kato with Attached Address of Count Uchida

subfiles.about: Internal State Department memorandum reporting that Japanese public schools teach anti-American sentiment citing the 1924 immigration exclusion.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck relays Salisbury's report that Japanese public schools teach children the United States is unjust, citing the 1924 Immigration Act's exclusion provision.
subfiles.title: Memorandum Regarding Anti-American Teaching in Japanese Public Schools

subfiles.about: Personal letter from Ambassador Grew to Secretary Stimson warning of manufactured war psychology in Japan, enclosing an Embassy memorandum on extensive army war preparations.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew alerts Secretary of State Henry L. Stimson that the Japanese Foreign Office and military are deliberately inciting public animosity against the United States to build up a war psychology, drawing parallels to imperial Germany in 1914. Grew highlights Japan's deteriorating economic and financial realities, arguing that the Manchurian venture represents military weakness rather than enduring national strength. An enclosed Embassy memorandum details extensive war preparations, including round-the-clock arsenal operations, increased imports of strategic raw materials, War Minister Sadao Araki's inflammatory propaganda, central bank currency expansions, and the subjugation of civilian politicians after Premier Inukai's assassination.
subfiles.title: Letter from Ambassador Grew to Secretary Stimson Regarding War Psychology and Army Preparations

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet noting Tokyo Despatch No. 106 on the rise of a German-style war psychology under the Japanese military hierarchy.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references Despatch No. 106 (790.94/30), August 26, 1932: the military is building a war psychology like Germany's before 1914.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Despatch No. 106 from Tokyo on Japanese War Psychology

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet recording a periodic report from Tokyo on the influence of the military in Japanese internal affairs.
subfiles.summary: Indexes a September 1932 Tokyo periodic report (894.00-P.R./57) on the military's growing influence in Japanese domestic affairs.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Periodic Report on Military Influence in Internal Affairs

subfiles.about: Extract from Tokyo Despatch No. 105 assessing the military's temporary tolerance of civilian politicians and the budgetary limits of the Manchurian campaign.
subfiles.summary: Extract from Despatch No. 105: the army leaves government to politicians but keeps detachments for order. Manchuria's costs leave little for rural relief.
subfiles.title: Extract from Despatch No. 105: Influence of the Military in Japan

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for a confidential memorandum by Stanley K. Hornbeck analyzing Japanese political conditions that could generate conflict with the United States.
subfiles.summary: Records Hornbeck's confidential September 12, 1932 memorandum (711.94/724) on Japanese factional politics that could cause friction with the United States.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Hornbeck Memorandum on U.S.-Japan Difficulties

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet recording Harbin Despatch No. 5515 transmitting political memoranda on the Tokyo political crisis and the Japanese gendarmerie.
subfiles.summary: Indexes Harbin Despatch No. 5515 (893.01-Manchuria/504) forwarding political memoranda on the Tokyo crisis and the Japanese gendarmerie in Harbin.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Harbin Despatch No. 5515 Transmitting Political Memoranda

subfiles.about: Despatches from Consul General Hanson at Harbin transmitting field intelligence memoranda on the Tokyo crisis and the role of the Japanese gendarmerie.
subfiles.summary: Consul General Hanson at Harbin forwards translated intelligence memoranda on the Tokyo political crisis and the Japanese gendarmerie in Harbin, via Minister Johnson at Peiping.
subfiles.title: Harbin Despatch No. 5515 Transmitting Despatch No. 2401 to Peiping with Political Memoranda

subfiles.about: Routing memorandum from Stanley K. Hornbeck submitting Tokyo Embassy's monthly political review No. 145 to Under Secretary Castle.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck routing slip to Castle with Tokyo Despatch No. 145, noting the monthly review arrived early and he marked key sections.
subfiles.title: Memorandum Routing Tokyo Monthly Review No. 145

subfiles.about: State Department summary of Tokyo Despatch No. 130 analyzing Kenzo Adachi's newly organized Kokumin Domei party.
subfiles.summary: Salisbury on Despatch No. 130: Adachi's new Kokumin Domei showed influence in the Diet session, but its state-control platform carries little weight.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 130 Regarding the Kokumin Domei

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew's report on Kenzo Adachi's Kokumin Domei party, enclosing its founding declaration, platform, and policy outline.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew details the formation of the Kokumin Domei (National League or People's League), founded by former Home Minister Kenzo Adachi after his resignation brought down the Wakatsuki Cabinet. Grew observes that the recruitment of thirty Lower House members from the Minseito has left the rival Seiyukai with an absolute legislative majority. Enclosed translations provide the Kokumin Domei's formal declaration, three-plank platform, and thirteen-point policy outline demanding state control of major industries, the establishment of a Japan-Manchukuo economic bloc, an independent judiciary, and the coordination of diplomacy with armaments.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 130: The Kokumin Domei, A New Political Organization

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet recording Tokyo Despatch No. 145 on the Japanese political situation during September 1932.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references Despatch No. 145 (894.00-P.R./58), October 4, 1932: Japan's internal politics in September were comparatively quiet.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Despatch No. 145 on Political Situation for September 1932

subfiles.about: Extract from Tokyo Despatch No. 145 analyzing parliamentary maneuvers, the death of Minseito leader Tasuku Egi, and army political organizing.
subfiles.summary: Describes Japanese politics after the September 5 Diet adjournment: the Seiyukai majority hesitates to topple Saito fearing fascism; the Minseito weakens; Araki courts the Ex-Servicemen's Association.
subfiles.title: Extract from Despatch No. 145: Internal Political Activity during September 1932

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet recording Paris Report No. W.D. 1114 concerning Japan being virtually ruled by a military dictatorship.
subfiles.summary: Indexes Paris Report W.D. 1114 (893.01-Manchuria/590): European information that Japan is ruled by an unchecked military dictatorship.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Paris Report W.D. 1114 on Japanese Military Dictatorship

subfiles.about: Paris Embassy report conveying French intelligence assessments of Japanese anti-Bolshevik policy in Manchuria and military dominance in Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: Dawson reports French sources: fear of Bolshevism drives Japan in Manchuria, and a de facto military dictatorship would overthrow any civilian cabinet changing the status quo. France might recognize Manchukuo.
subfiles.title: Paris Despatch No. 1210 Transmitting Report No. W.D. 1114 on the Far Eastern Situation

subfiles.about: Routing note by Stanley K. Hornbeck praising Tokyo Despatch No. 165 as the most significant report received in eight months.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck's routing memo calls Tokyo Despatch No. 165 the most significant analytical report the Far Eastern Division has received in eight months.
subfiles.title: Memorandum by Hornbeck Evaluating Tokyo Despatch No. 165

subfiles.about: Departmental analysis of Tokyo Despatch No. 165 assessing indications of moderate revival against the Japanese military clique.
subfiles.summary: Salisbury summarizes Despatch No. 165: Makino resisted ouster, Debuchi returned to Washington, and Ugaki was floated to replace Saito. Military may still provoke war with Russia or annex North China.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 165 Regarding Growth of Moderate Tendencies in Japan

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew's comprehensive despatch analyzing evidence of growing civilian moderation and covert resistance to the Japanese military.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew evaluates the undercurrent of moderate opinion in Japan resisting the aggressive military faction. While open dissent has been suppressed since late 1931—exemplified by the hounding of Dr. Inazo Nitobe and arrests of anti-imperialist protesters—Grew identifies emerging counter-pressures, including Count Makino's retention as Lord Keeper of the Privy Seal, outspoken editorials in the Japan Times, and rumors favoring General Ugaki as Premier to curb War Minister Araki. An enclosed memorandum from Diplomatic Secretary H. M. Benninghoff details a conversation between his father, Rev. H. B. Benninghoff, and an editor of Chuo Koron revealing that prominent intellectuals are flooding publishers with critical anti-war manuscripts that cannot be printed due to police censorship. Grew warns that while moderates are gaining confidence, fanatical junior officers might plunge the nation into external disaster rather than relinquish power.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 165: Growth of Moderate Tendencies in Japan

subfiles.about: Letter from Colonel Landers of the 99th Division inquiring about the delayed arrival of the two-volume Japanese White Book.
subfiles.summary: Colonel Landers of the 99th Division asks whether the Japanese White Book was delayed; it has not arrived in Pittsburgh.
subfiles.title: Letter from Colonel Landers Inquiring on Japanese White Book Delivery

subfiles.about: Letter from Stanley K. Hornbeck to Colonel Landers explaining an administrative delay in sending the Japanese White Book.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck apologizes for a clerical error and confirms the two-volume Japanese White Book has now been sent to Colonel Landers.
subfiles.title: Letter from Hornbeck to Colonel Landers Clarifying Shipment of Japanese White Book

subfiles.about: Initial letter from Colonel Landers requesting a copy of the Japanese White Book for army officer research on the Far East.
subfiles.summary: Colonel Landers requests the Japanese White Book for officers at Pittsburgh headquarters studying Far Eastern developments.
subfiles.title: Letter from Colonel Landers Requesting the Japanese White Book
subfiles.to: Far Eastern Division, Department of State

subfiles.about: Letter from Stanley K. Hornbeck forwarding a two-volume Japanese White Book on China, Manchuria, and Mongolia to Colonel Landers.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck sends Colonel Landers the two-volume Japanese White Book obtained from the Japanese Embassy.
subfiles.title: Letter from Hornbeck Transmitting Japanese White Book to Colonel Landers

subfiles.about: Departmental summary of Tokyo Despatch No. 180 concerning an inflammatory circular circulated among army officers by an extremist patriotic society.
subfiles.summary: Salisbury on Despatch No. 180: an extremist circular from an Osaka society incites junior officers against Ugaki and Makino. It reveals assassination plots and shows military radicalism.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 180 Regarding Extremist Military Circular

subfiles.about: Despatch transmitting a translated circular distributed by the Dai Nankokai of Osaka inciting junior officers against General Ugaki and Count Makino.
subfiles.summary: Chargé d'Affaires ad interim Edwin L. Neville transmits a translated circular distributed by the Dai Nankokai (Association of Patriots) of Osaka among Japanese army divisions. The circular urges junior officers to oppose General Kazunari Ugaki and Imperial Household adviser Count Nobuaki Makino, labeling Ugaki a traitor for reducing military appropriations and suppressing the October plot. It praises the assassins of Premier Inukai, details court-martial proceedings involving Sub-Lieutenant Murayama and Lieutenant Koga's targeting of Makino, and exposes the involvement of nationalist writer Shumei Okawa.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 180: Circular Distributed by the Dai Nankokai of Osaka
